entry: Writings in the Latin language, including essays, histories, poems and plays. Formal Latin literature began in 240 BC, when the first Latin stage play was performed in Atella, a town in Campania south of Rome. Early authors adapted Greek works: Livius Andronicus translated Homer's *Odyssey* into Latin, and Quintus Ennius wrote the historical epic *Annals*. Plautus and Terence wrote comedies, and 20 of the 26 surviving early Latin comedies are by Plautus. Cato the Elder wrote the first Latin history of Rome. The golden age, traditionally dated from 81 BC to AD 17, produced [[Cicero]], [[Virgil]], [[Ovid]] and [[Horace]]. Latin remained the lingua franca of Western and Central Europe through the Middle Ages, and European writers after the fall of the Roman Empire, including [[Thomas Aquinas]], [[Francis Bacon]], [[Baruch Spinoza]] and [[Isaac Newton]], also wrote in Latin.

Writing system based on the letters of the classical Latin alphabet, also called the Roman script. Its ancestor was a form of the [[Greek alphabet]] used in the ancient Greek city of Cumae, which the Etruscans altered and the ancient Romans later changed. The script is the basis of the [[International Phonetic Alphabet]] and the basis for the largest number of alphabets of any writing system. It is the standard method of writing the languages of Western and Central Europe, most of sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas and Oceania, as well as many other languages. Its spread followed the [[Roman Empire]] from the Italian Peninsula to the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. The 26 most widespread letters form the ISO basic Latin alphabet, which matches the English alphabet. The American Standard Code for Information Interchange ([[ASCII]]) included the 26 × 2 uppercase and lowercase letters, and later [[Unicode]] standards extended the set to other letters.

Geographic coordinate specifying the north-south position of a point on the surface of the Earth or another celestial body. It is given as an angle from −90° at the [[South Pole]] to 90° at the [[North Pole]], with 0° at the [[Equator]]. Lines of constant latitude, called parallels, run east-west as circles parallel to the equator. Latitude and [[Longitude]] are used together as a coordinate pair. On its own, the term normally refers to geodetic latitude, the angle between the perpendicular to an ellipsoidal reference surface and the plane of the equator. Because there are many reference ellipsoids, a precise latitude is not unique without a specified coordinate reference system. Precise measurement requires an understanding of the Earth's gravitational field, the subject of [[Geodesy]], and latitude is determined in celestial navigation with the meridian altitude method.

Genus of spiders, informally called widow spiders, with 34 species. Its members include several North American black widows, the European black widow, the [[Redback spider|redback spider]] of Australia and the New Zealand katipō. Their venom contains the neurotoxin latrotoxin, which causes latrodectism, and only the bites of females are dangerous to humans. About 2,500 people in the United States report bites each year, but most do not need medical treatment. A 2012 review found no deaths from black widows in the United States since 1983.

Country in the Baltic region of northern Europe, one of the three [[Baltic states]] along with [[Estonia]] and [[Lithuania]]. Its capital and largest city is [[Riga]], and it has a population of 1.83 million. Latvians make up 65.5% of the population, and Russians, the most prominent minority, account for almost a quarter. After centuries under Teutonic, Swedish, Polish-Lithuanian and Russian rule, the independent Republic of Latvia was established on November 18, 1918, after breaking away from the Russian Empire. Soviet incorporation at the outset of World War II was followed by German occupation in 1941 and Soviet re-occupation in 1944. Independence was restored on August 21, 1991, and Latvia has since been a democratic unitary parliamentary republic. It is a developed country with a high-income economy and a member of the [[European Union]], [[NATO]] and the [[United Nations]].

Rocket-powered vehicle designed to carry a payload, such as a crewed [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]] or [[Satellite|satellites]], from Earth's surface or lower atmosphere to [[Outer space|outer space]]. The most common form is a multistage rocket shaped like a ballistic missile, and most launch vehicles operate from a launch pad. An orbital launch vehicle must lift its payload at least to the boundary of space, about 150 km (93 mi), and accelerate it to a horizontal velocity of at least 7,814 m/s (17,480 mph). Practical orbital vehicles use chemical propellants such as solid fuel, liquid hydrogen, kerosene or liquid oxygen. [[NASA|NASA]] classifies vehicles by [[Low Earth orbit|low Earth orbit]] payload capacity, from small-lift vehicles below 2,000 kilograms to super-heavy-lift vehicles above 50,000 kilograms. Expendable vehicles are designed for one-time use, while reusable vehicles such as the [[SpaceX]] Falcon 9 are recovered and launched again.

Washing of [[Clothing|clothing]] and other textiles, along with their drying and ironing. Laundry has been part of history since humans began to wear clothes, and it has traditionally been highly gendered, with women responsible in most cultures. Early laundering took place in watercourses, where flowing water carried away stains and smells, and the cloth was rubbed, twisted or slapped against flat rocks. Villages across Europe later built communal wash-houses, often with two basins, one for washing and one for rinsing, which became meeting places for women. The [[Industrial Revolution]] led to mechanized solutions, notably the [[Washing machine|washing machine]] and later the tumble dryer. Laundry is still done both at home and by commercial establishments; a self-service laundry is called a launderette in British English or a laundromat in North American English.

American actress, the daughter of actors Bruce Dern and Diane Ladd. She rose to prominence in David Lynch's films *Blue Velvet* (1986) and *Wild at Heart* (1990). Her role as an orphan in *Rambling Rose* (1991) earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress. Her role as Ellie Sattler in Steven Spielberg's [[Jurassic Park]] (1993) brought international recognition, and she reprised it in later sequels. She won a Primetime Emmy Award for *Big Little Lies* and the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as a divorce lawyer in *Marriage Story* (2019).

American writer, teacher and journalist, best known for the children's book series *Little House on the Prairie*, published between 1932 and 1943. The series was based on her childhood in a settler and pioneer family. She grew up partly in the Big Woods region of [[Wisconsin]], and her family moved repeatedly during her childhood, living in Wisconsin, [[Kansas]] and Minnesota. Her first book, *Little House in the Big Woods* (1932), was set in the Pepin area of Wisconsin where her family had lived.

English-American comedy duo active as a double act from 1927 to 1955. Englishman Stan Laurel and American Oliver Hardy began in the [[Silent film|silent film]] era, transitioned easily to talking pictures and became internationally famous for slapstick comedy. Laurel, a former [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] performer, played a clumsy, childlike character, while Hardy played a domineering and genteel one. Their theme song, known as "The Cuckoo Song", was heard over the opening credits of their films. They appeared as a team in 107 films, including 23 full-length features, and their sole American television appearance was on the [[NBC]] program *This Is Your Life* on December 1, 1954.

American actress and one of the last surviving major stars of Hollywood's Golden Age. She made her film debut at the age of 19 in *To Have and Have Not* (1944) opposite [[Humphrey Bogart]], whom she later married. She appeared with Bogart in film noir such as *The Big Sleep* (1946) and *Key Largo* (1948),. She earned the Golden Globe Award for *The Mirror Has Two Faces* (1996). On Broadway she won two Tony Awards for Best Actress in a Musical, for *Applause* (1970) and *Woman of the Year* (1981).

English actor and director, one of four male actors who dominated the British stage in the mid-20th century, alongside [[John Gielgud]], Michael Redgrave and Ralph Richardson. His first major West End success was in Noël Coward's *Private Lives* (1930). In 1935 he appeared in a celebrated production of [[Romeo and Juliet]] with Gielgud, and in the 1940s he co-directed the Old Vic, building it into a respected company. From 1963 to 1973 he was the founding director of Britain's National Theatre. He directed and starred in *Hamlet* (1948), and he received an Academy Award for his on-screen work. Olivier was knighted in 1947 and made a life peer in 1970. He married the actress [[Vivien Leigh]] from 1940 to 1960.

American actress and comedian known for stage, television and film work. She played Jackie Harris on [[Roseanne]], for which she won three Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series. She has won three Tony Awards, including Best Actress in a Play for *A Doll's House, Part 2* (2017) and Best Featured Actress in a Play for the revival of *Three Tall Women* (2018). Her performance as a mother in *Lady Bird* (2017) earned an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress. From 1995 to 2019 she voiced Andy's mom in the *Toy Story* films.

American rapper, singer and songwriter, and frontwoman of the Fugees. Their second album, *The Score* (1996), sold over 22 million copies worldwide and won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Album, making Hill the first woman to receive the honor. Her solo debut, *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* (1998), debuted atop the Billboard 200. At the 41st Annual [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]], Hill became the first rapper to win Album of the Year and the first woman to win five awards in a single night. She has received eight Grammy Awards, the most for any female rapper.

Molten rock expelled from the interior of a terrestrial planet or moon onto its surface. Lava may erupt at a [[Volcano|volcano]] or through a fracture in the crust, on land or underwater, usually at temperatures of 800 to 1,200 °C (1,470 to 2,190 °F). A lava flow is an outpouring of lava during an effusive eruption, whereas an explosive eruption produces a mixture of volcanic ash and other fragments called tephra. The [[Viscosity|viscosity]] of most molten lava is about that of [[Ketchup|ketchup]], roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times that of water, yet lava can flow great distances because exposed lava quickly forms a crust that insulates the liquid beneath. Silica content largely determines viscosity: felsic lavas have a silica content greater than 63% and are extremely viscous, so they usually erupt explosively. The word comes from Italian, where it originally described a stream caused by sudden rain.

Genus of 47 known species of perennial flowering plants in the sage family, [[Lamiaceae|Lamiaceae]], commonly called lavender. Native to the Iberian Peninsula, the Mediterranean coastline, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent, its members are cultivated as ornamental plants and culinary herbs, and commercially for essential oils. Lavender is used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] and as an ingredient in cosmetics. Around 93 phytochemicals have been identified in lavender oil, including linalyl acetate (30–55%) and linalool (20–35%). [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] combined the European species, which had been considered separate genera, into one genus, and in *Species Plantarum* (1753) he recognized only five species.

Soviet politician and head of the NKVD secret police from 1938 to 1945 under [[Joseph Stalin]]. He organized the [[Katyn massacre]] of 22,000 Polish officers and intelligentsia, and oversaw mass deportations of ethnic minorities from the Caucasus in 1943–44, which many scholars describe as ethnic cleansing or genocide. From 1945 he oversaw the Soviet atomic bomb project. After Stalin's death in March 1953 he briefly led the country as part of a triumvirate, and an amnesty freed nearly half of the Gulag's inmates. He was removed in a coup in June 1953, tried for treason and executed.

American police procedural and legal drama television series created by [[Dick Wolf|Dick Wolf]]. It aired on [[NBC|NBC]] from September 13, 1990, to May 24, 2010, and was revived in 2022 after an 11-year hiatus. Set and filmed in [[New York City|New York City]], each episode has two halves: police detectives investigate a crime and arrest a suspect, and the Manhattan district attorney's office then prosecutes the case. Plots are based on real cases that made headlines. The series has won numerous Primetime Emmy Awards.

Mathematical law of probability theory stating that the average of results from a large number of independent random samples converges to the true value. A casino may lose money on a single spin of a roulette wheel, but its earnings tend toward a predictable percentage over many spins. The law applies only when many observations are considered: a streak of one outcome is not immediately balanced by the others. The [[Expected value|expected value]] of a six-sided die roll is 3.5, and the average of many rolls approaches 3.5 as more dice are rolled. Similarly, the proportion of heads in many fair coin flips approaches 1⁄2. The law underlies the [[Monte Carlo method]], which relies on repeated random sampling. The average of results from some heavy-tailed distributions, such as the Cauchy distribution, does not converge. The law is used in statistics, probability theory, economics and insurance.

Part of international law that regulates the conditions for initiating war and the conduct of hostilities. It includes *jus ad bellum*, which governs the right to use force and includes the crime of aggression, and *jus in bello*, the law applicable during wartime. Modern rules address declarations of war, the treatment of prisoners of war, the principles of distinction, military necessity and proportionality, and the prohibition of weapons that cause unnecessary or excessive suffering. The first traces of such law appear in the [[Code of Hammurabi|Code of Hammurabi]] of 1750 BC, and [[Augustine of Hippo|Augustine of Hippo]] wrote on the doctrine of just war. The four [[Geneva Conventions|Geneva Conventions]] of 1949 are the foundational modern instruments, and violations can be prosecuted before the [[International Criminal Court|International Criminal Court]].

Device that uses one or more revolving blades, or a reel, to cut grass to an even height. The lawn mower was invented in 1830 by Edwin Beard Budding of Stroud, Gloucestershire, England, as a superior alternative to the scythe for cutting grass on sports grounds and extensive gardens. Budding received a British patent on August 31, 1830. Rotary mowers use a single blade that rotates about a vertical axis, while reel mowers use a cutting cylinder that rotates about a horizontal axis. Power comes from human effort, an [[Electric motor|electric motor]] or a small four-stroke, typically one-cylinder, [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]]. Robotic mowers operate autonomously, and the largest multi-blade mowers are mounted on [[Tractor|tractors]] for golf courses and municipal parks.

Epic biographical drama film directed by David Lean, released in 1962. It is based on the life of [[T. E. Lawrence|T. E. Lawrence]] and his 1926 book *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*. Peter O'Toole plays Lawrence, with Alec Guinness as Prince Faisal. The film depicts Lawrence's role in the Arab revolt against Ottoman rule in Hejaz and Syria during the First World War, including attacks on Aqaba and [[Damascus|Damascus]]. At the 35th [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] in 1963 it was nominated for ten Oscars and won seven, including Best Picture and Best Director. The [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]] deemed it "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" in 1991, and it was selected for the National Film Registry.

Set of physical laws defining quantities such as temperature, energy and entropy in systems at thermodynamic equilibrium. The zeroth law defines thermal equilibrium and forms the basis for temperature: if two systems are each in equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other. The first law states that a system's internal energy changes with work and heat in accordance with the conservation of energy. The second law states that the sum of the [[Entropy|entropies]] of interacting systems never decreases, so heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder body to a warmer one. The third law states that a system's entropy approaches a constant value as temperature approaches [[Absolute zero|absolute zero]]. The first and second laws prohibit perpetual motion machines of the first and second kinds.

Civil action in which one or more parties, the plaintiff or claimant, proceed against one or more parties, the defendant, in a court of law. A plaintiff claims to have suffered loss from a defendant's actions and requests a legal or equitable remedy. The defendant must respond to the complaint or risk a default judgment. If the plaintiff succeeds, the court may award damages or restitution, or issue an [[Injunction|injunction]] to prevent or compel an act, and a declaratory judgment may be issued to prevent future disputes. Conducting a civil action is called litigation, and the parties are called litigants. About 98 percent of civil cases in United States federal courts are resolved without a [[Trial|trial]].

Person qualified to offer advice about the law, draft legal documents and represent individuals in legal matters. The work varies by jurisdiction and area of practice. The role can be traced back to ancient [[Greece|Greece]] and [[Rome|Rome]]. In many jurisdictions the profession is divided into branches such as [[Barrister|barristers]], solicitors, conveyancers, notaries and canon lawyers. England developed a division between barristers, who argue before higher [[Court|courts]], and solicitors, who prepare cases and advise clients; the [[United States|United States]] and [[India|India]] fused these roles. Education can range from an undergraduate law degree to postgraduate training, and passing a bar examination is necessary in many jurisdictions before practice.
